abstract: The ability to grow fast and develop frugally in the face of hazards is a common feature of plants and animals. Life History Theory predicts that trade-offs between immediate survival or reproduction and future longevity may occur under threatening conditions. Embryos of the Neotropical red-eyed treefrog (Agalychnis callidryas) hatch prematurely (escape hatching) in response to ecological stressors such as flooding-induced hypoxia, desiccation, and egg-predator attack, making this species an ecologically grounded model for the evolutionary-developmental biology of early life stress (ELS). To assess the physiological correlates of ELS in A. callidryas, we bred nine captive adults in a rain chamber and divided ten resulting clutches into sibling-matched Early-Hatch (EH, N = 80; hatching induced by mechanical stimulation upon appearance of the keratinized beak) and Late-Hatch (LH, N = 99; undisturbed) groups. Tadpoles were harvested, measured, and weighed for cross-sectional growth analyses, with subsets used for morphometric and transcriptomic study. Cross-sectional mass-age trajectories differed between treatments: fitted EH mass rose early and peaked near 12 days post-hatching, whereas fitted LH mass increased throughout the shared 17-day observation interval. Derivative analyses consistently supported a later LH mass-age slope advantage, while evidence for an early EH advantage and greater EH deceleration depended on spline flexibility. Age- and family-adjusted morphometrics (32 EH, 35 LH) revealed treatment differences in overall size but not size-independent shape. Gene expression analyses of  three sibling-matched pairs identified 258 differentially expressed transcripts suggestive of a delay in adaptive immune system development and increased oxygen and antioxidant demands in EH. Threatened A. callidryas embryos do not merely hatch early: their premature entry into tadpole life initiates a developmental program of early compensatory growth followed by pronounced deceleration, accompanied by transcriptional differences consistent with life-history trade-offs between immediate survival and later development.

summary: Early escape hatching in red-eyed treefrog embryos alters tadpole growth trajectories and transcriptomes, suggesting life-history trade-offs under stress.
